To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) women with breast cancer are more anxious than their partners, 2) women's anxiety is associated with partners' perceptions of relationship quality, but not vice‐versa, 3) partners' perceptions of quality are associated with partners' distress, and 4) partners' distress is associated with women's well being.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of cancer on the family.
the impact of breast cancer on the quality of life of women and their spouses.
the role that social relationships play in shaping and moderating the experience of stress.

this article is a good one.
the findings of this study support the idea that the relationship between partners is a dynamic system that is interdependent.
there is a positive correlation between the level of anxiety experienced by a woman with breast cancer and the level of anxiety her partner experiences.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the distress of the patient with breast cancer was significantly related to that of their partner, and that the distress of both partners was related to perceptions of relationship quality.

the more the partners of women with breast cancers are distressed, the more distressed the woman with cancer is, and the more distress the woman with breast cancer is, the more distress the partner is.
we found that the partners' anxiety was a significant predictor of the woman's own anxiety and that the relationship quality of the couple was a significant mediator of that relationship.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the anxiety experienced by a woman with breast cancer is associated with the anxiety of her partner.
the distress experienced by a woman with breast cancer is associated with that of the partner.
partners' anxiety is a key predictor of women's anxiety, but not vice versa.
